In Figure 2 we set forth an algorithmic diagram of an Analytic and Intelligent Strategy (AIS).  

This diagram (Fig. 2) represents a structured approach to decision-making that combines data analysis with intelligent reasoning. Think of AIS as a roadmap for solving complex industrial problems. It likely includes stages like data collection, preprocessing, analysis, decision rules, and feedback loops. While we can’t see the details of the diagram here, the idea is to create a systematic process where information flows logically from raw data to actionable insights—possibly incorporating tools like fuzzy logic or expert systems at key decision points.

Fig. 2. Algorithmic diagram of AIS.  

We have set up a case study applying Fuzzy networks based on AIS and on SAI and on ERP and ES concepts previously analyzed.  

Note: “SAI” appears to be a typo or undefined acronym—possibly meant to be “AIS” again or another related term. Since it’s not defined in the chunk, we proceed cautiously, assuming it refers to a previously discussed intelligent system framework.

Fuzzy logic is a powerful methodology for solving specific issues (including case studies), offering a multitude of applications in controlling and information processing. This powerful methodology gives us an effective way to draw precise conclusions stemming from vague, ambiguous, or imprecise pieces of information.  

Here’s a simple analogy: imagine driving through fog. You can’t see clearly—everything is “fuzzy.” But you still make decisions: slow down a bit, stay in the lane, watch for shadows. You’re not working with exact data, but you’re using experience to interpret uncertainty. Fuzzy logic does the same for machines. Instead of requiring exact thresholds (e.g., “if temperature > 1500°C, then shut down”), it allows rules like “if temperature is very high, then reduce power slightly.” These linguistic variables—“very high,” “slightly”—are mathematically modeled using **fuzzy sets**, where membership isn’t all-or-nothing. For example, 1480°C might be “partially” in the “very high” category, allowing smoother, more human-like control.

Fuzzy logic based applications can lead to any of its potential benefits, such as: performance, productivity, simplicity and lower costs (Figure 3).  

These benefits arise because fuzzy systems can handle real-world messiness without needing perfect data. They’re often simpler to design than traditional control systems because they encode expert knowledge directly. In manufacturing, this might mean more stable processes, fewer defects, less energy waste—all contributing to lower costs and higher output.

The Fuzzy networks principle is to use neural networks and fuzzy set theory for modelling practical systems.  

A **Fuzzy network**—also known as a **neuro-fuzzy system**—combines the learning power of neural networks with the interpretability of fuzzy logic. Neural networks are great at finding patterns in data, but they’re often “black boxes”—hard to understand. Fuzzy systems are transparent (you can see the rules), but they rely on experts to define those rules. A Fuzzy network merges the best of both: it can learn from data like a neural network, but organizes that knowledge into human-readable fuzzy rules. This makes it ideal for industrial applications where both accuracy and explainability matter.

The algorithm related to a Fuzzy network is implemented as an inference engine that can automatically deduce precise conclusions from certain facts (data).  

An **inference engine** is the “brain” of the system. It takes input data (e.g., sensor readings), matches them against fuzzy rules (e.g., “if pressure is high and temperature is rising, then risk is high”), and produces an output (e.g., a warning or control action). The process involves several steps: fuzzification (converting crisp numbers into fuzzy values), rule evaluation, aggregation of results, and defuzzification (turning the fuzzy output back into a clear, actionable value). The result? A system that mimics expert judgment—even when the inputs aren’t perfect.

Equity-linked policy is an insurance or assurance policy in which a proportion of the premiums paid are invested in equities.  

In other words, part of your insurance payment doesn’t just go into a safety fund—it’s used to buy stocks or shares. This means the policy’s value can grow over time based on market performance, unlike traditional policies that offer fixed returns.

The surrender value of the policy is therefore the selling price of the equities purchased.  

If you decide to cancel (or “surrender”) the policy early, you don’t get a fixed refund—you get the current market value of the investments made on your behalf. So if the stock market has gone up, you could gain more; if it’s down, you might get less than you paid in.

As more premiums are paid the portfolio gets larger.

## Visual Evoked Field Responses to Checkerboard Pattern-Reversal: The Role of Check Size and Interstimulus Interval

When we look at a visual stimulus—like a flickering checkerboard—our brain generates electrical activity that can be measured using techniques such as visual evoked potentials (VEPs) or, in this case, visual evoked fields (VEFs) with magnetoencephalography (MEG). One of the most reliable signals in this response is a large positive wave that peaks around 100 milliseconds after the stimulus appears. In MEG studies, this is called the **P100m**; in EEG, it's known as the **P100**. But what determines how strong or fast this signal is? Two key factors explored in this study are the *size* of the checks in the checkerboard and the *timing* between successive stimuli—the interstimulus interval (ISI).

Let’s start by understanding how **check size** influences brain responses.

### How Check Size Influences Which Brain Cells Respond

Imagine the checkerboard you're viewing is made up of alternating black and white squares. The size of these squares—called "check size"—determines how detailed the pattern is. Scientists describe this in terms of **spatial frequency**, which is just a fancy way of saying "how many light-dark transitions occur across a given distance in your visual field."

- **Large checks** (e.g., 180' or 450') mean **low spatial frequency**: few transitions, broad patterns.
- **Small checks** (e.g., 15' or 30') mean **high spatial frequency**: many transitions, fine details.

Now here’s the crucial point: your retina isn’t uniform. Different parts of it are specialized for different jobs.

- The **periphery** of the retina (outside the center) is great at detecting large, coarse patterns—like spotting movement in your side vision.
- The **fovea**, the very center of your retina, is packed with cells that detect fine detail—like reading small text.

So when you see **large checks**, they mainly activate cells in the **peripheral retina**. These signals travel to the **anterior (front) part of the striate cortex**—the brain’s primary visual area in the occipital lobe. This pathway turns out to be especially effective at generating the **P100m** response.

On the flip side, **small checks** (high spatial frequency) fall mostly on the **fovea**, activating foveal retinal cells. These connect to the **posterior (back) striate cortex**, near the occipital pole. While this setup is ideal for sharp vision, it's *less effective* at producing a strong P100m. Instead, it tends to elicit the classic **P100** seen in EEG studies.

This distinction helps explain why large checks are more powerful for evoking P100m in MEG experiments—they tap into a neural pathway optimized for coarse, peripheral processing.

### What Does the VEF Waveform Look Like?

In this study, the visual evoked field (VEF) response to reversing checkerboards typically showed a **triphasic wave complex**—that is, three main bends in the signal over time. The most prominent of these is the second deflection, which peaks at about **100 milliseconds**. This pattern matches what earlier studies have labeled the **N75m-P100m-N145m complex**, where:

- **N75m** is a negative wave peaking around 75 ms,
- **P100m** is a large positive wave at ~100 ms,
- **N145m** is a later negative wave at ~145 ms.

Even though this study didn’t record EEG simultaneously, the researchers reasonably assume that the **P100m** they measured corresponds directly to the **P100** seen in EEG studies. Why? Because the timing and sequence match: a negative wave before (~70 ms), a big positive peak at ~100 ms, and another negative wave after (~150 ms). Previous studies that *did* record both MEG and EEG found **no significant difference in latency** between P100m and P100, suggesting they arise from the same underlying cortical activity—likely in the primary visual cortex.

Supporting this link, the average P100m latency observed here for **30' checks** was **115.0 ms** (see Table 1), which closely matches the **118.8 ms** reported in a prior MEG study using **28' checks** under similar conditions. This consistency across studies strengthens confidence in the reliability of these measurements.

### Small Checks: Weaker and Slower Responses

When the researchers used **smaller checks (15')**, they observed two clear effects:

1. **Smaller amplitude** (weaker signal),
2. **Delayed peak latency** (slower response).

This finding isn’t new—it aligns with earlier VEP studies and a recent MEG study. But *why* does this happen?

To understand this, we need to think about the **retinal ganglion cells**—the neurons in your retina that send visual information to your brain. These cells aren’t all the same. Those most sensitive to **high spatial frequencies** (fine details) are concentrated in the **fovea**. They have two key features:

- **Small receptive fields**: they monitor a tiny patch of visual space,
- **Small-diameter axons**: their nerve fibers are thin, which means they conduct signals more slowly.

Because of this, when you present small checks (high spatial frequency), you're primarily activating these **slow-conducting, fovea-centered cells**. That helps explain the **delayed latency** of the P100m response: the signal simply takes longer to reach the brain.

Moreover, because these cells cover a smaller area and respond less vigorously to large-scale contrast changes, the overall **amplitude** of the brain response is reduced. So, even though small checks provide more detail, they’re actually *less efficient* at driving the kind of widespread neural synchronization needed for a strong P100m—especially when the stimulus is presented in the periphery.

This fits with the idea of **parallel visual processing**: your brain processes different aspects of vision (like detail vs. motion) through separate but simultaneous pathways. Large checks engage the fast, coarse-processing pathway (via peripheral retina), while small checks rely on the slower, detail-oriented foveal pathway.

### What Happens with Very Large Checks (>120')?

Interestingly, the effects of **very large checks**—like 180' or even 450'—haven’t been widely studied. One prior MEG study by Nakamura and colleagues found that **180' checks** produced a slightly **longer latency** and **smaller amplitude** compared to **90' checks**.

In this study, the results were even more pronounced: P100m responses to **180' and 450' checks** showed **progressive weakening** compared to **120' checks**. That is, bigger wasn’t better—beyond a certain point, increasing check size actually *reduced* the brain’s response.

Why might this happen? The researchers offer two compelling explanations.

#### Explanation 1: Too Few Pattern Cycles

Think of each black-white pair in the checkerboard as one **cycle** of a visual pattern. The number of complete cycles across the visual field matters. In this experiment:

- **120' checks** provided about **six full cycles**,
- **180' checks** gave only **five cycles**,
- **450' checks** had just **two cycles**.

Now, here’s a key insight from vision science: the visual system needs a **minimum number of cycles** to reliably detect a pattern. Studies using colored sine-wave gratings (smoothly varying red/green patterns) have shown that **fewer than six cycles** lead to **weaker visual responses**, even if the contrast is high.

So, the **optimal response at 120' checks** may not be about size per se, but about hitting that **"sweet spot" of six cycles**—enough for the brain to clearly recognize and respond to the repeating pattern. Larger checks fall short in this regard, offering too few cycles to drive a strong response.

#### Explanation 2: Mixing of Visual Channels

There’s another possibility: very large checks might activate different **visual processing channels** in the brain.

Your visual system has multiple pathways, including:

- **Luminance channels**: sensitive to brightness differences,
- **Contrast channels**: tuned to edges and pattern changes.

Typically, pattern-reversal stimuli (like flipping a checkerboard) are designed to isolate **contrast-specific responses**. But with **very large checks**, the brain may start interpreting the stimulus more as a **global brightness change** rather than a detailed pattern. This could **activate luminance-sensitive pathways**, which aren’t as effective at generating the typical P100m.

In other words, the signal becomes "contaminated" by non-pattern-specific activity, diluting the contrast-driven response. Supporting this idea, earlier studies on retinal responses have shown that **large checks can evoke non-specific electrical activity** in the retina that isn’t tied to pattern processing.

So, the attenuation of P100m with very large checks might reflect a shift from **pattern-specific** to **luminance-dominated** processing—a kind of neural "mismatch" between what the stimulus intends to probe and what the brain actually responds to.

### Check Size Also Affects Earlier Components: The Case of N75

So far, we’ve focused on P100m, but check size doesn’t just affect this one wave. It also influences earlier components like **N75** (or N75m in MEG).

Multiple VEP studies have shown that as check size increases:

- **N75 amplitude decreases**,
- **N75 latency shortens**.

Like P100/P100m, N75m is also modulated by factors like **aging** and **contrast level**, suggesting it reflects meaningful neural processing in the visual cortex.

Given this, studying how **check size affects N75m** in MEG could provide deeper insight into the early stages of visual processing. However, in this particular study, the researchers chose not to analyze N75m. Why?

Because when they used a wide range of check sizes, the **N75m response was often too weak or inconsistent to measure reliably** (see Figure 1). Without clear, reproducible signals, drawing firm conclusions would be risky. So while the topic is scientifically interesting, the data limitations prevented further exploration here.

### Does Timing Between Stimuli Matter? The ISI Effect on P100m

Finally, what about the **interstimulus interval (ISI)**—the time between one checkerboard reversal and the next?

This factor has been understudied in MEG. One earlier VEP study found that when ISI increased from **0.25 seconds to 1 second**, the P100 latency **shortened by 4.8 ms**—suggesting that longer breaks between stimuli allow the brain to respond faster.

But in this study, **no significant change** in P100m activation was observed across different ISIs. That is, whether stimuli came quickly or slowly, the brain’s response (in terms of latency and amplitude) stayed roughly the same.

The Impact of the Finite Element Method on Medical Device Design  
Mark Driscoll¹  
Published online: 6 June 2018  
© Taiwanese Society of Biomedical Engineering 2018  

Over the last 10 years, medical device design has vastly benefited from the integration of finite element analyses in the product development process. But what exactly is the *finite element method* (FEM), and why has it become such a game-changer in this field? Let’s break it down step by step.

At its core, the finite element method (FEM) is a powerful numerical technique used to solve complex engineering and physical problems—specifically, boundary value problems. Think of a boundary value problem as a real-world scenario where we want to understand how something behaves (like stress in a bone or blood flow in an artery), but only if we know the conditions at its edges or boundaries (like how much force is applied or what the pressure is at the ends). These problems are governed by partial differential equations—mathematical expressions that describe how physical quantities change in space and time. Solving them exactly is often impossible for real-life geometries, which is where FEM comes in.

So how does FEM work? Instead of trying to solve the equations for the entire complex structure all at once, FEM breaks the structure down into thousands—or even millions—of tiny, manageable pieces called *finite elements*. These elements are connected at specific points called *nodes*. The method then computes how each small piece responds to forces, pressures, or other loads, and how those responses interact across the entire system. It's like solving a giant puzzle by first understanding each tiny piece and then seeing how they fit together to form the full picture.

For medical device design, this approach is transformative. Engineers can build a digital twin—a virtual 3D model—of a medical device (like a stent, hip implant, or spinal screw) and simulate how it will behave inside the human body. This virtual domain is carefully designed to mimic real-life biological conditions, such as the stiffness of bone, the pulsing of blood, or the movement of joints. By running FEM simulations, designers can predict how the device will perform *before* ever building a physical prototype.

This means a user can leverage FEM results not just to see *if* a device works, but *how well* it works—and where it might fail. These insights allow engineers to interpret device performance with high precision and make educated, data-driven recommendations for improvement and optimization [1–3]. For example, if a simulated hip implant shows high stress concentrations in a certain region, the design can be modified to redistribute that stress, potentially preventing fractures in real patients.

But FEM’s power doesn’t stop at initial performance. One of its most exciting applications is predicting *long-term* behavior in the body—what we call *in vivo* performance. The human body is dynamic: tissues remodel, loads change over time, and implants interact with living systems in complex ways. To capture this, engineers often use *multi-scaled and iterative analyses* [4, 5]. This means running simulations at different levels of detail (from the whole implant down to the microscopic structure of bone) and repeating the process with updated conditions—like how a bone might adapt to an implant over months or years. These predictions help researchers anticipate complications and refine designs to improve safety and longevity.

As a result, when it comes time to conduct actual animal or human studies (*in vivo* testing), the team is much better prepared. They’re not guessing in the dark; they’re testing informed hypotheses. This can lead to more efficient, ethical, and successful clinical trials [6, 7].

However, none of this is possible without a crucial ingredient: *an experienced user working within an interdisciplinary team*. FEM is not a push-button tool. It requires deep understanding of mechanics, material behavior, computational methods, and—just as importantly—biological systems. A mechanical engineer might build a perfect simulation, but without input from a surgeon or biologist, the model might miss critical real-world factors like tissue healing or patient variability. So, the team must include experts from different fields who can collectively interpret the results and ensure the simulation truly reflects clinical reality.

This brings us to a key point: FEM is more than just software. It’s a *virtual test platform*—a digital laboratory where ideas can be tested, refined, and validated with speed and precision. And as this platform continues to grow in popularity, teams that master it gain a significant advantage in innovation and efficiency.

Now, let’s talk about *why* FEM has become so attractive in medical device development. The advantages are numerous, but perhaps the most compelling is *speed*. Traditionally, designing a new medical device involved building multiple physical prototypes, testing them in the lab (bench testing), and iterating based on results. This process is not only slow but also expensive—each prototype can cost thousands of dollars, and testing setups require specialized equipment and time.

FEM changes this equation entirely. With a well-constructed model, engineers can simulate device performance in *silico*—on the computer—within hours or days, not weeks or months. This allows for rapid exploration of design alternatives: “What if we change the thickness here?” “What if the material is slightly softer?” These “what-if” scenarios can be tested virtually, dramatically accelerating the early design phase.

As a result, the integration of FEM into product development can significantly *reduce costs* over the entire development cycle. How? By reducing the number of physical prototypes needed and minimizing the number of bench testing iterations. Instead of building five versions of a device to find the best one, you might build only one or two—because the rest were already tested and optimized in simulation.

In essence, FEM allows you to do bench testing *without* the bench—*in silico* instead of *ex vivo* (outside the living body) or on physical test stands. This doesn’t mean physical testing becomes obsolete—far from it. Real-world validation is still essential. But FEM ensures that when you do test physically, you’re testing a much more refined, well-understood design.

Yet, for all its benefits, FEM is not without challenges. The biggest disadvantage? The *high level of expertise* required to use it correctly. FEM software is powerful, but it’s also unforgiving. If you input incorrect material properties, oversimplify a boundary condition, or mesh the geometry too coarsely, the simulation might run perfectly—but give completely wrong results. And because the output often looks so polished (with colorful stress maps and smooth animations), it’s easy to be misled by “beautiful garbage.”

This risk is especially high in medical applications, where biological systems are inherently complex and variable. An inexperienced user might make *ambitious misinterpretations*—drawing strong conclusions from a model that doesn’t accurately represent reality. That’s why proper training and rigorous methodology are non-negotiable.

Moreover, adopting FEM isn’t just about learning new software—it requires a shift in *product development strategy*. Companies must integrate FEM into the *early design phase*, not just use it as a final check. This means investing in training, computational resources, and interdisciplinary collaboration from day one. For many organizations, especially smaller ones, this transition demands considerable effort and cultural change.

Because of these barriers, FEM has not yet fully shaken off the perception of being a *research tool*—something academics use in labs—rather than a core *development asset* used routinely in industry. But as more success stories emerge and best practices become standardized, that perception is slowly shifting.

So, how does one become a skilled and experienced FEM user? It starts with a deep understanding of the *mechanics behind the solver*—the mathematical engine that crunches the numbers. You don’t need to write the code yourself, but you *do* need to understand how it works: what assumptions it makes, how it handles nonlinearities, and how it converges to a solution.

Equally important is a strong commitment to *verification and validation*—two concepts that are often confused but are fundamentally different. Let’s clarify them.

*Verification* asks: **"Are we solving the equations correctly?"** In other words, is the software accurately computing the mathematical solution to the model you’ve built? Most commercial FEM software (like ANSYS, Abaqus, or COMSOL) undergoes rigorous verification by the developers before release. But that doesn’t mean your *specific model* is correct. You still need to verify that your implementation—especially any custom material models or user-defined subroutines—is working as intended.

For example, if you’re simulating a soft biological tissue, you might use a special *constitutive formulation*—a mathematical model that describes how the tissue deforms under load. These formulations can be highly complex, capturing nonlinear elasticity, viscoelasticity, or anisotropy (different behavior in different directions). Before trusting your results, you must verify that this formulation is coded correctly and that the solver converges properly under various conditions.

But here’s a subtle but critical point: even if each individual component is verified, *combining them can introduce new errors or instabilities*. For instance, a material model might work fine on its own, and a contact algorithm might work fine on its own—but when used together in a simulation of a joint implant, they might interact in unexpected ways, causing the solution to diverge or oscillate. These *compounded relations* must also be verified and carefully documented.

Once verification is complete, the next step is *sensitivity analysis* or *probabilistic analysis*. These techniques help you understand how sensitive your results are to the assumptions you’ve made—like the exact value of a material’s stiffness or the magnitude of an applied load. You intentionally vary these inputs within a reasonable range and observe how much the output (e.g., stress or displacement) changes.

If the results fluctuate wildly with small changes in input, that’s a red flag. It means your conclusions are highly dependent on assumptions that may not be precisely known—so you must select those variable values very carefully, and interpret the results with caution. On the other hand, if the results remain stable despite variations, your model is *robust*, and your conclusions are more trustworthy.

Now, let’s turn to *validation*. This asks a different question: **"Are we solving the right equations?"** In other words, does your model accurately represent the real-world physics of the problem? Verification ensures the math is correct; validation ensures the *physics* is correct.

The gold standard for validation is *experimental testing*. You design a physical experiment that closely matches the conditions of your FEM simulation—a real-world version of the same boundary value problem. For example, if you simulated a spinal implant under compression, you’d test an actual implant in a mechanical testing machine under the same loading conditions.

If the experimental results (e.g., how much the implant deforms) match the simulation results, your model is validated—or at least supported—for that specific scenario. If they don’t match, you need to go back and refine your assumptions: maybe the material model is wrong, or the boundary conditions don’t reflect reality.

This kind of direct validation is the most convincing way to build confidence in your FEM results. But the user must be aware of *statistical variances* that

books.l5:
## Data Analysis

Before we begin analyzing the data, it’s important to understand how the key variable—**IgE** (Immunoglobulin E)—was handled. IgE is a type of antibody involved in allergic responses and defense against parasites. In this study, IgE levels were originally measured in nanograms per milliliter (ng/ml), but to make comparisons easier across studies and populations, they were converted into **international units (IU)** using a standard conversion:  
> **1 IU = 2.4 ng/ml**

This means if someone had an IgE level of 2.4 ng/ml, that would be exactly 1 IU/ml. This conversion ensures consistency with other scientific literature.

Now, here’s a crucial point: IgE levels in human populations don’t follow a normal “bell curve” distribution. Instead, they are **log-normally distributed**—meaning most people have relatively low IgE levels, but a few individuals have very high values, which pulls the distribution to the right (it’s skewed). You can see this clearly in Figure 1, where the data for all three populations—Tsimane, Shuar, and NHANES—show this characteristic skew.

👉 *Why does this matter?*  
Because many common statistical tests (like t-tests) assume that the data are normally distributed. If we use them on raw IgE values, we risk getting misleading results. To fix this, we apply a **natural logarithm transformation** (written as **lnIgE**) to the data. This transformation "pulls in" the extreme high values and makes the distribution much closer to normal, satisfying the assumptions of our statistical tools.

So from this point forward, unless otherwise noted, all analyses use **lnIgE**, the log-transformed version of IgE.

When reporting results like means from these transformed data, we can’t just report the average of the lnIgE values and call it a day—that wouldn’t make intuitive sense to readers who think in terms of actual IgE concentrations. Instead, we calculate **geometric means**. Here's how:

- We take the mean of the **lnIgE** values (which is valid statistically),
- Then we **exponentiate** that mean (i.e., compute $ e^{\text{mean of lnIgE}} $) to convert it back to the original scale.

This gives us the **geometric mean**, which represents a kind of "average" IgE level that respects the skewed nature of the data. For example, if the mean lnIgE is 3, then the geometric mean IgE is $ e^3 \approx 20 $ IU/ml. This is different from the arithmetic mean, which would be inflated by outliers.

All descriptive statistics and t-tests were performed using **PASW Statistics 18.0** (formerly known as SPSS), a widely used software package for social sciences and biomedical research. All other analyses—including more advanced modeling—were conducted in **R 2.10.1**, a powerful open-source programming environment for statistical computing (available at www.r-project.org).

---

To explore how IgE levels change with age in each population, the researchers used **Generalized Additive Models (GAMs)** [43,44]. Let’s unpack what that means.

Traditional linear models assume relationships are straight lines: for example, “IgE increases by X units per year.” But biology is rarely that simple. The relationship between IgE and age might rise quickly in early childhood, plateau in adulthood, or even decline later in life. GAMs are perfect for this kind of situation because they allow us to model **non-linear, smooth patterns** without forcing the data into a rigid shape.

Think of it like drawing a freehand curve through a scatterplot that captures the overall trend—except the computer does it mathematically, choosing the best-fitting smooth line based on the data.

In this study, the GAMs were fitted using the `gam` function in R’s **mgcv** package, which is one of the most popular tools for this type of analysis. The models used **thin plate regression splines** [45,46]—a fancy name for a flexible mathematical method that creates smooth curves by piecing together polynomial functions, minimizing roughness while staying close to the data.

But here’s a challenge: the number of participants in each population wasn’t evenly spread across ages. For instance, there might be many adults but very few young children in one group. If we placed model "knots" (points where the curve can change direction) at equal age intervals, some regions would have too little data to estimate the curve reliably.

To solve this, the researchers set the initial **basis knots** based on **even percentiles of the age distribution**—specifically, every 10%. That means there’s roughly the same number of people between each pair of knots. This ensures that each segment of the curve is supported by a similar amount of data, improving the reliability of the fit. You can visualize this setup in Figure 2.

Once the knot locations were set, the model automatically determined the **smoothing parameters**—essentially, how wiggly or smooth the final curve should be—using the default settings in the `gam` function [45]. This prevents overfitting (where the curve follows noise instead of the true pattern).

Each GAM included several components:
- An **intercept** (the baseline level),
- A **sex factor** (to account for differences between males and females),
- A **spline for age** (to capture the overall non-linear trend),
- And a **spline for the age-by-sex interaction** (to allow the pattern of change with age to differ between males and females).

This last term is especially important—it lets the model ask: *Does IgE rise faster in boys than in girls? Do women’s levels peak earlier than men’s?* Without this interaction, we’d assume both sexes follow the same age trajectory, which might not be true.

---

When the researchers first ran these models, here’s what they found:

For the **Shuar** and **NHANES** populations, the models predicted similar IgE levels at birth:
- **Shuar**: ~7 IU/ml for females, ~9 IU/ml for males
- **NHANES**: ~15 IU/ml for females, ~21 IU/ml for males

These values aren’t identical, but they show a consistent pattern: males start slightly higher than females, and both groups have measurable IgE at birth.

However, the **Tsimane** model behaved differently. Because there were relatively few Tsimane children under five years old, the model didn’t have enough data to detect any curvature in the early years. As a result, the initial fit was essentially a straight line—with the **highest IgE level predicted at birth**, and then a steady decline with age.

But wait—does that make biological sense?

Multiple previous studies have shown that **IgE levels at birth are extremely low—typically less than 1 IU/ml** [47–52], even in babies born to mothers with high IgE due to parasitic infections [53,54]. Newborns haven’t yet been exposed to most environmental triggers or parasites, so their immune systems haven’t started producing much IgE.

Given this strong biological expectation—and the fact that both the Shuar and NHANES models showed low but detectable levels at birth—the researchers decided to **anchor the Tsimane model to a more realistic starting point**.

They did this by adding **dummy cases**—artificial data points—with the following properties:
- Age = 0 (birth)
- IgE = 15 IU/ml (converted to lnIgE for analysis)

These dummy cases were included **only in the GAM models**, not in any other statistical tests. Their purpose was to "pull" the beginning of the curve down toward a biologically plausible value, helping the spline fit a more realistic shape despite the lack of real infant data.

It’s like putting a pin at birth to hold the curve in place while letting the rest of it flex according to the real data. This technique is a common workaround when data are sparse in critical regions, as long as the anchoring is justified by external evidence—which it clearly is here.

---

Beyond GAMs, the researchers also used a **binomial logit-link GAM** to estimate the **odds ratios of helminth infection by age** in the Tsimane population. This model helps answer: *How does the probability of having a parasitic worm infection change as people get older?* By using a logit link, the model ensures predictions stay within valid probability bounds (between 0 and 1), while still allowing for smooth, non-linear age trends.

Additionally, to examine how **helminth infections relate to IgE levels**, the team used **linear models** (on lnIgE) that controlled for:
- Infection with other types of helminths (to isolate effects),
- Sex,
- And age.

This way, they could ask: *Even after accounting for age and sex, do people with worms tend to have higher IgE?*

---

To double-check the age-related patterns seen in the GAMs and to compare populations more directly, two additional analytical approaches were used.

The first was a **stepwise linear regression with dummy variables** designed to detect sharp changes in IgE levels at specific ages. Here’s how it worked:

For each unique age in the dataset (e.g., 1, 2, 3... years), a **dummy variable** was created that indicated whether a person was **older than that age**. For example, the dummy for age 5 would be 0 for everyone 5 or younger, and 1 for everyone older than 5.

## The effect of soluble solids on flow activation energy

When we heat or cool a liquid like fruit juice, its thickness—what scientists call *viscosity*—changes. But how easily it flows when heated also depends on what’s dissolved inside it. In the case of enzyme-clarified Indian gooseberry juice, one key factor is the amount of **soluble solids**, which is mostly sugar and other plant compounds. These are measured in degrees Brix (°Bx), a unit that tells us how much dissolved material is in the juice.

Now, when we want to understand how temperature affects the flow of this juice, we use a concept called **flow activation energy**, or $ E_a $. Think of $ E_a $ like a “flow barrier”: the higher the $ E_a $, the more energy (in the form of heat) you need to get the molecules moving and the juice flowing. It’s similar to how much effort you’d need to push a heavy box across a rough floor—the rougher the floor (or the thicker the liquid), the more energy you need.

So, how do the dissolved sugars affect this energy barrier? Researchers tested two mathematical models to describe how $ E_a $ changes as the concentration of soluble solids increases. These models help us predict the behavior of the juice under different conditions—essential for designing industrial processes like pasteurization or bottling.

### Two models for flow activation energy

The first model is the **power law** equation:

$$
E_a = a (C)^b, \tag{3}
$$

The second is the **exponential-type** equation:

$$
E_a = a \exp(b C), \tag{4}
$$

Let’s unpack these.

- $ E_a $: This is the **flow activation energy**, measured in joules per mole (J mol⁻¹). It tells us how sensitive the flow of the juice is to temperature changes.
- $ C $: This stands for **soluble solids content**, given in °Brix. It’s the independent variable—the thing we’re changing to see how $ E_a $ responds.
- $ a $ and $ b $: These are **fitting parameters**, or constants that are adjusted so the equation best matches the experimental data. They don’t have a direct physical meaning on their own, but their values tell us about the strength and nature of the relationship between concentration and energy.

Now, why choose one model over the other? That’s where data fitting comes in.

Using the **method of least squares**, scientists plugged in the measured values of $ E_a $ and $ C $ to find the best possible values for $ a $ and $ b $ in both equations. This method minimizes the total difference between the predicted values from the equation and the actual lab measurements—like drawing the smoothest line through scattered data points.

The results, summarized in Table 4 (not shown here), revealed something important: the **exponential model (Equation 4)** described the data better than the power law model (Equation 3). How do we know? By looking at the **correlation coefficient**, denoted $ R $, which measures how closely the model matches the data. A value of $ R = 1 $ means a perfect fit.

- For the exponential model: $ R > 0.9954 $
- For the power law model: $ R < 0.9875 $

Since the exponential model has a higher $ R $, it captures the trend more accurately. This suggests that the relationship between soluble solids and flow activation energy isn’t just a simple power relationship—it grows faster, in a way that an exponential function can better describe. In practical terms, this means that each additional increment of sugar has a *compounding* effect on the energy needed to make the juice flow.

### Why does concentration affect viscosity and flow?

But why does adding more soluble solids make the juice harder to flow in the first place?

Even before we consider temperature, increasing the concentration of soluble solids **increases the viscosity** of the juice. This happens because more dissolved molecules—like sugars and organic acids—interact with water through **hydrogen bonding**. These molecules have hydroxyl (–OH) groups that attract water molecules, forming a kind of "hydration shell" around them. As more of these hydrated molecules are packed into the juice, they get in each other’s way, making the liquid thicker.

Moreover, higher concentration leads to **increased particle aggregation**. The dissolved molecules start to cluster together, increasing the number and strength of interactions between them. This network of interactions resists flow, raising viscosity. And this effect happens **regardless of temperature**—though temperature can reduce viscosity by giving molecules more energy to break free from these interactions.

This strong, **non-linear** effect of solids on viscosity is well-documented in Newtonian fluids (fluids whose viscosity doesn’t change with applied force), as noted by Krokida et al. (2001).

### Modeling viscosity directly

Since viscosity itself is so sensitive to concentration, researchers also used two similar equations to model how **viscosity ($ \eta $)** changes with soluble solids content at fixed temperatures:

**Power law model:**
$$
\eta = a (C)^b, \tag{5}
$$

**Exponential-type model:**
$$
\eta = a \exp(b C). \tag{6}
$$

Here, $ \eta $ (eta) is the viscosity in millipascal-seconds (mPa·s), and the rest of the symbols mean the same as before.

Again, the parameters $ a $ and $ b $ were estimated using the **least squares method** at different temperatures, and the results are shown in Table 5. Once more, the **exponential model outperformed** the power law model. The correlation coefficients ($ R $) for the exponential model ranged from **0.9887 to 0.9951**, indicating an excellent fit across all temperatures.

This consistency across models and conditions tells us something powerful: the way dissolved solids affect the physical behavior of fruit juices isn’t linear or simple—it’s **exponentially sensitive**. Small increases in sugar content can lead to disproportionately large increases in viscosity and flow resistance.

This insight is crucial for food engineers. For example, when designing heat exchangers or pumps, knowing that viscosity rises exponentially with concentration helps in selecting the right equipment and energy inputs. It also explains why concentrated juices behave so differently from diluted ones, even at the same temperature.

Now, let’s look at the actual viscosity measurements taken at different soluble solids levels and temperatures.

From this table, we can see a clear pattern: at any given temperature, **viscosity increases as soluble solids increase**. For example, at 20°C, viscosity jumps from 5.30 mPa·s at 8.2°Bx to 7.94 mPa·s at 35.9°Bx—a nearly 50% increase. That’s a big change in flow behavior from just increasing sugar content.

We can also see that **as temperature increases, viscosity decreases**—which makes sense because heat gives molecules more energy to overcome intermolecular forces. But even at high temperatures, the juice with 35.9°Bx is still much thicker than the dilute version at low temperature.

This dual dependence—on both **temperature** and **concentration**—is why modeling is so important. It allows us to predict viscosity under any combination of conditions, which is essential for quality control and process optimization.

## 5.1 Simulation Studies

To compare the global performance of the different estimators we consider, we need a way to measure how close an estimated probability distribution is to the true underlying distribution. For each set of parameters $\theta = (\mu, \sigma, \lambda)$, we use a powerful and intuitive measure called the **total variation distance (TVD)**. This tells us, in a precise sense, how "far apart" two probability distributions are.

### What is Total Variation Distance (TVD)?

Let’s break this down. Suppose we have:
- A **true** probability density function $f_{\theta_0}(y)$, which describes the real data-generating process.
- An **estimated** density $f_\theta(y)$, based on our estimator using sample data.

The total variation distance between these two densities is defined as:

$$
\text{TVD}(\theta) = \int |f_\theta(y) - f_{\theta_0}(y)| \, dy
$$

🧠 **What does this mean intuitively?**  
Imagine plotting both density curves on the same graph. At every point $y$, you look at the vertical gap (absolute difference) between the two curves. The TVD adds up all those gaps across the entire range of possible values. It's like measuring the total "area between the curves." 

✅ The smaller this area, the more similar the two distributions are.  
✅ If the estimated density perfectly matches the truth, TVD = 0.  
✅ The maximum possible value of TVD is 2, but since densities integrate to 1, the actual maximum difference is bounded by 1 in meaningful comparisons.

So, **TVD quantifies the overall discrepancy between what we estimated and what is actually true**, making it an excellent global measure of estimation quality.

---

### Measuring Estimator Performance: Mean Total Variation Distance (MTVD)

Now, any estimator $\hat{\theta}$ (like maximum likelihood or a robust alternative) will give slightly different results each time due to random sampling. So we don’t just evaluate one estimate—we want to know how well the estimator performs *on average*.

We define the **Mean Total Variation Distance (MTVD)** of an estimator $\hat{\theta}$ as:

$$
\text{MTVD}(\hat{\theta}) = \mathbb{E}\left[\text{TVD}(\hat{\theta})\right]
$$

📌 Here, the expectation $\mathbb{E}$ means: "average over many repeated samples from the same true model."

In other words, we simulate many datasets from the true model, apply our estimator to each, compute the TVD for each resulting estimate, and then take the average. This gives us a stable, reliable measure of how good the estimator is *in the long run*.

Since we can’t compute this expectation exactly in practice, we approximate it using simulation. With $N$ simulated replications of the estimator $\hat{\theta}_k$ (for $k = 1, 2, \dots, N$), we calculate the **Average Total Variation Distance (ATVD)**:

$$
\text{ATVD}(\hat{\theta}) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{k=1}^N \text{TVD}(\hat{\theta}_k)
$$

This ATVD is our empirical estimate of MTVD. The larger $N$, the more accurate this approximation becomes.

💡 **Why use TVD instead of something simpler like mean squared error?**  
Because TVD evaluates the *entire shape* of the estimated density, not just specific moments. Two densities can have the same mean and variance but very different shapes (e.g., one bimodal, one unimodal). TVD catches such differences—making it a more comprehensive diagnostic tool.

---

## 5.1.1 Simulation under the Nominal Model

We now study how well the estimators perform when the data come exactly from the assumed model—the so-called **nominal model**. This is the "best-case scenario" where all assumptions hold.

We considered sample sizes $n = 50, 100, 400,$ and $1000$, and true shape parameters $\lambda_0 = 1$ and $\lambda_0 = 2$. Without loss of generality (since location and scale can be standardized), we set the true location and scale parameters to $\mu_0 = 0$ and $\sigma_0 = 1$.

We also examined two levels of **censoring**: 15% and 25%. Censoring occurs when some observations are only partially observed (e.g., in survival analysis, we know a patient survived up to a certain time, but not beyond). This adds complexity to estimation.

For each configuration, we ran $N = 1200$ simulation replications to ensure stable estimates of ATVD.

📊 **Figure 1 (top)** shows a particularly insightful comparison: it plots the **ATVD of robust estimators divided by the ATVD of the Maximum Likelihood (ML) estimator**, as a function of sample size, for $\lambda = 1$ and 15% censoring.

🔁 This ratio is called the **TVD efficiency**—a form of relative efficiency:
- A value **less than 1** means the robust estimator performs *better* than ML (in terms of TVD).
- A value **close to 1** means the robust estimator performs almost as well as ML.
- A value **greater than 1** means it’s worse.

🎯 **What do we expect?**  
Under the nominal model (i.e., no outliers, perfect model fit), the ML estimator is theoretically optimal—it should achieve the lowest possible variance among consistent estimators. So we expect ML to have the smallest ATVD, meaning other estimators should have TVD efficiency ≥ 1.

🔍 **What do we observe?**
- The robust estimators—labeled 1TML, 2TML, and 1SWML—have TVD efficiencies **markedly greater than 1** for small samples (e.g., $n=50$), meaning they’re less efficient than ML when the model is correct.
- But as the sample size increases, their TVD efficiency **approaches 1**. That is, they become nearly as good as ML in clean data.

✅ This is excellent news for robust methods!  
Even though they’re designed to handle contamination, they don’t pay too high a price in clean data—they are **asymptotically efficient**. As $n$ grows, they "catch up" to ML.

🔄 Similar patterns were observed across other settings ($\lambda_0 = 2$, 25% censoring), confirming that this behavior is consistent.

📌 **Takeaway**: These robust estimators strike a smart balance—they may sacrifice a bit of efficiency in ideal conditions, but they gain resilience when things go wrong (as we’ll see next).

---

## 5.1.2 Simulation under Point Mass Contamination

Now let’s stress-test the estimators. What happens when the data aren’t perfect? In real-world applications, datasets often contain **outliers**—erroneous or extreme observations that don’t follow the assumed model.

To simulate this, we conducted a second Monte Carlo experiment with **point mass contamination**. This is a classic and challenging way to introduce outliers.

Here’s how it works:
- 90% of the data (“good” observations) are generated from the true Generalized Log-Gamma (GLG) model.
- 10% of the data (“outliers”) are placed at a fixed point $y_0$, creating a spike (or “point mass”) in the distribution.

We varied $y_0$ from $-10$ to $10$ in steps of $0.5$, effectively sliding the outlier cluster across the real line to test how sensitive each estimator is to the location of contamination.

🎯 **Why use point mass contamination?**  
It’s considered one of the **most adverse forms of contamination** because it creates a sharp, concentrated deviation from the model. If an estimator can withstand this, it’s likely to perform well under more diffuse or realistic outlier scenarios.

We again used $n = 50, 100, 400, 1000$, $\lambda_0 = 1$ and $2$, and censoring fractions of 15% and 25%. For each value of $y_0$, we performed 1200 replications.

📊 **Figure 1 (bottom)** displays the **ATVD of the estimated densities** as a function of $y_0$. This shows how the overall estimation error changes depending on where the outliers are located.

🔍 **Key Findings**:
- The estimators **TQ$\tau$ (with 10% trimming), 1TML, and 2TML** show remarkably **stable ATVD values** across all values of $y_0$. Their performance barely wavers whether outliers are on the far left ($y_0 = -10$), center, or far right ($y_0 = 10$).
- In contrast, the **1SWL estimator** exhibits a **very high ATVD for positive values of $y_0$**—indicating it breaks down badly when outliers appear in the upper tail.
- The **ML estimator** is so sensitive to outliers that its ATVD becomes extremely large—so large, in fact, that it’s **not shown** in the plot. Its behavior is **unbounded**: a single outlier can completely distort the ML estimate.

🧠 **Why does ML fail so badly?**  
Maximum likelihood assumes every data point comes from the model. When even 10% of the data are wildly off, ML tries to "explain" them by drastically shifting the estimated parameters. This leads to massive bias.

🛠️ **How do the robust estimators resist this?**
- **TQ$\tau$** uses trimming: it automatically down-weights or removes the most extreme 10% of residuals, effectively ignoring the outliers.
- **1TML and 2TML** are two-step robust procedures: they first identify and reduce the influence of outlying observations before re-estimating the model.
- **1SWL**, unfortunately, lacks sufficient protection against asymmetric contamination, especially in the upper tail, which explains its poor performance.

📌 **Takeaway**: Under contamination, robustness matters. While ML fails catastrophically, properly designed robust estimators maintain stable, reliable performance—exactly what we need in practical data analysis.

---

## 5.2 Regression Case

We now extend our evaluation to a more complex and realistic setting: **regression with censored responses**.

A second set of experiments was run to investigate the behavior of:
- The **MM-TQ$\tau$** estimator (defined in Section 4.1),
- The **1TML** and **2TML** estimators (defined in Section 4.2),
- And the **1SWL** estimator (defined in Section A.3.2 of the Appendix).

In each simulation, we generated $n$ pairs of observations $(x_i, y^*_i)$ according to the following regression model:

$$
y_i = \mu_0 + \beta_0^\top x_i + \sigma_0 u_i, \tag{34}
$$
$$
y^*_i = \min(y_i, c_i), \tag{35}
$$
$$
c_i = \mu_c + e_i, \tag{36}
$$
$$
\delta_i = 
\begin{cases} 
1 & \text{if } y^*_i = y_i \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \tag{37}
$$

Let’s unpack this step by step.

📌 **Equation (34)**: This is the **true regression model**.
- $y_i$: the latent (unobserved) response variable.
- $x_i = (x_{i1}, x_{i2})$: a vector of two predictors.
- $\beta_0^\top = (2, 3)$: the true regression coefficients.
- $u_i$: random error drawn from a GLG distribution with parameters $(\mu=0, \sigma=1, \lambda=\lambda_0)$, where $\lambda_0 = 1$ or $2$.
- $\mu_0 = 0$, $\sigma_0 = 1$: location and scale of the error term.

📌 **Equation (35)**: This introduces **right-censoring**.
- $y^*_i$: the observed response.
- $c_i$: the censoring threshold.
- If the true $y_i$ exceeds $c_i$, we only observe $c_i$, not the full value. This mimics scenarios like survival times where a patient is still alive at the end of the study.

📌 **Equation (36)**: The censoring threshold $c_i$ itself varies across individuals:
- $\mu_c$: a fixed baseline.
- $e_i \sim \text{GLG}(\mu_c, 1, 1)$: random variation in censoring times.

📌 **Equation (37)**: The indicator $\delta_i$ tells us whether observation $i$ is censored ($\delta_i = 0$) or fully observed ($\delta_i = 1$).

🎯 **Goal**: Estimate the regression parameters $(\mu_0, \beta_0, \sigma_0, \lambda_0)$ accurately despite censoring and potential outliers.

The predictors were generated as:
- $x_{i1} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$: a continuous covariate (standard normal),
- $x_{i2} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(0.4)$: a binary covariate (e.g., treatment vs. control),
- Independent of each other.

the achiral structure of the bar-type nanoslits cannot distinguish the helicity of light.  
This means that whether the incoming light is right-handed (clockwise rotation of the electric field) or left-handed (counterclockwise), the bar-shaped nanostructures respond in exactly the same way. They lack any inherent "handedness" or chirality in their design—like a plain straight road that doesn’t care which direction you turn onto it. As a result, they cannot tell the difference between the two circular polarizations, denoted as $|\sigma_+\rangle$ (right-handed) and $|\sigma_-\rangle$ (left-handed). This symmetry limitation prevents them from exhibiting polarization-dependent responses, such as selectively enhancing or suppressing one helicity over the other.

For the /C22Z-type metasurfaces, Fig. 5(a1,b1,c1,d1) shows SEM images of $q = 1, -1, 2,$ and $-2$, respectively. Let’s unpack what this means. The parameter $q$ refers to the topological charge of the metasurface, which essentially dictates how the orientation of the individual building blocks—called metamolecules—rotates as you move around the ring. A positive $q$ means the rotation follows a counterclockwise twist; a negative $q$, a clockwise twist. The magnitude tells us how many full rotations occur over one circumference. So for $q = 1$, the metamolecules complete one full turn around the ring; for $q = 2$, two turns, and so on.

Now, looking at these SEM images, we see that even though the metamolecules have been replaced—from simple bars to more complex /C22Z-shaped elements—the overall symmetry of the metasurface remains unchanged. In other words, the global geometric pattern still respects the same rotational symmetries as before. Specifically:
- The circular symmetry corresponds to $q = 1$,
- Square symmetry to $q = -1$,
- Linear (or bilateral) symmetry to $q = 2$,
- Hexagonal symmetry to $q = -2$.

This preservation of symmetry is crucial because it allows us to isolate the effect of the metamolecule’s shape—its local chirality—without being confounded by changes in the global geometry.

Under $|\sigma_+\rangle$ illumination (right-handed circularly polarized light), we observe specific near-field interference patterns via scanning near-field optical microscopy (SNOM), shown in Fig. 5(a2,b2,c2,d2), along with corresponding finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations in Fig. 5(a3,b3,c3,d3). Remarkably, the symmetry of the resulting surface plasmon polariton (SPP) field patterns still matches the geometric symmetry of each metasurface. This tells us that the macroscopic arrangement continues to guide the overall symmetry of the excited electromagnetic field.

However, the fine details—the intricate interference fringes—look very different from those seen with the bar-type metasurfaces. Why? Because now, each /C22Z-shaped metamolecule is itself chiral: it has a built-in handedness. In fact, these /C22Z units are planar chiral and specifically left-handed. Think of them like tiny spiral staircases etched flat into the surface, all turning in the same direction—say, like a left-handed screw when viewed from above.

When right-handed circularly polarized light ($|\sigma_+\rangle$) hits these left-handed chiral structures, something fascinating happens. The incident light tries to excite surface plasmons that carry a certain orbital angular momentum—a kind of "twist" in the wavefront. But because the metamolecule is left-handed, it naturally wants to generate a vortex-like SPP field that circulates in the opposite direction (counterclockwise, if we define the coordinate system appropriately).

This leads to a clash: the geometric phase induced by the metasurface structure and the spin-orbit interaction from the circular polarization produce fields with opposing circulation. When these two effects are out of sync—when the handedness of the light doesn’t match the handedness of the structure—they interfere destructively in the near field.

Nowhere is this more evident than in Fig. 5(a2): for the $q = 1$ metasurface under $|\sigma_+\rangle$ illumination, almost no SNOM signal is detected. That means there's very little light-matter interaction happening at the surface—very few plasmons are being excited. The simulation in Fig. 5(a3) confirms this: the calculated electric field intensity is extremely weak, roughly an order of magnitude lower than for the other cases. It’s as if the structure and the light are “speaking different languages”—they can’t communicate effectively.

Why does this destructive interference happen so strongly for $q = 1$ and not as completely for others? Because the $q = 1$ structure has circular symmetry, which supports the formation of a clean, coherent vortex field. When that ideal vortex is excited with the wrong helicity, the mismatch is total, leading to near-perfect cancellation. But for non-circularly symmetric structures—like the square ($q = -1$), linear ($q = 2$), or hexagonal ($q = -2$)—the symmetry breaks the perfection of the vortex. You can’t form a smooth, continuous whirlpool on a square-shaped track. So while some destructive interference still occurs, it’s incomplete. That’s why in Fig. 5(b3,c3,d3), we see residual fringe patterns lingering alongside the main symmetric features—“relics” of partial interference, where some plasmonic activity survives despite the mismatch.

But now, flip the polarization: use left-handed circularly polarized light, $|\sigma_-\rangle$, on the $q = 1$ metasurface. Suddenly, everything clicks. The incident light has the same handedness as the chiral metamolecules. Now, instead of fighting each other, the geometric phase and the spin-induced field reinforce one another. Constructive interference takes over. This is clearly seen in Fig. 5(a4,a5), where strong, well-defined interference fringes appear in both measurement and simulation. The structure and the light are now in harmony, efficiently coupling energy into the SPPs.

For the other symmetric metasurfaces [Fig. 5(b,c,d)], the near-field SPP patterns under $|\sigma_+\rangle$ illumination resemble those of the bar-type counterparts—but with completely different fringe details. This isn’t just random noise; it reflects the new physics introduced by the chiral metamolecules. The interference landscape is reshaped by the local chirality, making the response highly sensitive to the input polarization.

The big takeaway? Unlike the achiral bar-type designs, these chiral /C22Z metasurfaces *can* distinguish between left- and right-handed light. They respond strongly to one helicity and weakly (or not at all) to the other, depending on their structural handedness. This selective response based on spin—on the circular polarization state—is a hallmark of the **optical spin Hall effect**. It’s a direct manifestation of spin-orbit coupling in nanophotonics, where the "spin" of light (its polarization) influences the "orbit" (its spatial trajectory or mode structure) via structured interfaces.

It is noted that the results of the Z-type metasurface are completely opposite to those of the /C22Z-type one and are not shown here.  
This implies that the Z-type structures are likely right-handed chiral versions of the same design. So they would couple strongly to $|\sigma_+\rangle$ light and weakly to $|\sigma_-\rangle$, the reverse of /C22Z. This symmetry complementarity further underscores the role of structural chirality in controlling light at the nanoscale.

Entre as gestantes que realizaram o teste durante o pré-natal, o VDRL — um exame usado para detectar sífilis — foi positivo em 14 delas, o que corresponde a 1% do total. Dentre essas 14 gestantes com resultado positivo, metade (50%) tinham parceiros que também fizeram o teste VDRL, e, desses parceiros, 42,8% receberam tratamento adequado. Isso destaca a importância de envolver também os parceiros no diagnóstico e tratamento, já que a sífilis é uma infecção sexualmente transmissível e pode ser transmitida de volta à gestante se o parceiro não for tratado.

O antígeno de superfície do vírus da hepatite B (HbsAg) estava registrado no cartão de pré-natal de 1.198 parturientes. Nesse grupo, a prevalência de infecção crônica pelo vírus da hepatite B foi de 0,4%. Isso quer dizer que, a cada 1.000 gestantes, cerca de 4 tinham hepatite B de forma crônica. O intervalo de confiança de 95% (IC95%) — que nos dá uma faixa dentro da qual o valor real provavelmente está — foi de 0,36% a 0,44%, indicando que a estimativa é bastante precisa, com pouca margem de erro.

A idade média em que as gestantes tiveram sua primeira relação sexual foi de 16,5 anos, com um desvio padrão (DP) de 2,9 anos. O desvio padrão nos diz o quão variável é essa idade entre as mulheres: quanto maior o valor, mais espalhados estão os dados em torno da média. Neste caso, um DP de 2,9 sugere que a maioria das mulheres teve sua primeira relação sexual entre cerca de 14 e 19 anos (ou seja, dentro de um intervalo de aproximadamente dois desvios padrão da média).

A mediana da idade gestacional ao nascimento foi de 39 semanas, com um desvio interquartil (DIQ) de 37 a 40 semanas. A mediana é o valor central: metade das gestações durou menos que 39 semanas, metade durou mais. O desvio interquartil mostra onde estão os 50% do meio dos dados — aqui, entre 37 e 40 semanas — o que indica que a maioria das gestações estava bem próxima do termo completo (considerado entre 37 e 42 semanas).

Os dados socioeconômicos e demográficos das 1.380 parturientes estão detalhados na Tabela 1. Mais de um quarto delas — 25,5% — eram adolescentes (entre 13 e 19 anos), o que pode ter implicações importantes para o cuidado pré-natal, já que adolescentes grávidas podem enfrentar barreiras adicionais no acesso a serviços de saúde. A grande maioria (83,9%) tinha renda familiar de até três salários mínimos, o que reflete uma população predominantemente de baixa renda. Cerca de 55,7% das mulheres tiveram parto normal, enquanto os demais tiveram cesariana, abortamento ou necessitaram de tratamento clínico durante a internação.

Quase todas as parturientes — aproximadamente 95% — relataram ter feito pré-natal, o que é um indicador positivo de acesso aos serviços de saúde. No entanto, entre essas, 8,5% fizeram menos de quatro consultas, o que está abaixo do mínimo recomendado pela Organização Mundial da Saúde (pelo menos seis consultas). Apenas 54,8% realizaram seis ou mais consultas, o que sugere que, embora o acesso inicial ao pré-natal seja alto, a continuidade e a qualidade do acompanhamento podem ser insuficientes em muitos casos.

Os fatores de risco relatados pelas gestantes incluíram: história de doença sexualmente transmissível (DST) em 4,1% delas, transfusão sanguínea (3,2%), uso de drogas injetáveis (0,9%), uso de drogas não injetáveis (3,8%) e prática de prostituição (0,3%). A grande maioria — 89,3% — relatou ter tido apenas um parceiro sexual no último ano, o que é um comportamento considerado de menor risco para infecções como HIV e sífilis.

Alguns desses fatores se mostraram especialmente relevantes na análise de risco. História de DST e prática de prostituição estiveram associadas tanto ao HIV quanto à sífilis — ou seja, mulheres que relataram essas experiências tinham maior probabilidade de terem sido diagnosticadas com uma dessas infecções. Por outro lado, ter feito pré-natal e ter tido um único parceiro no último ano foram identificados como fatores de proteção: eles reduziram a chance de infecção, provavelmente por promoverem maior acesso a cuidados e testes, além de menor exposição a novos parceiros.

Outros fatores também mostraram associações específicas: o uso de drogas não injetáveis, ter um parceiro com sorologia positiva para HIV ou com histórico de encarceramento estiveram associados ao HIV. Já a história de violência sexual esteve associada à sífilis — uma ligação preocupante que pode refletir situações de vulnerabilidade e exposição forçada a riscos.

Essas associações são exploradas com mais detalhe na Tabela 2, que apresenta as razões de chances (OR — *odds ratio*) com intervalos de confiança de 95%. A OR nos diz o quanto um fator aumenta (ou diminui) a chance de uma infecção. Por exemplo, uma OR maior que 1 indica maior risco; menor que 1, proteção.

Apesar dessas associações observadas, o modelo final de regressão logística — uma técnica estatística usada para analisar a relação entre múltiplas variáveis e um desfecho (neste caso, infecção por HIV ou sífilis) — **não mostrou associação estatisticamente significativa** entre os fatores de risco estudados e as infecções. Isso pode parecer contraditório à primeira vista, mas é importante entender: enquanto algumas associações individuais parecem fortes (como a história de DST), quando todas as variáveis são analisadas juntas no modelo estatístico, os efeitos podem se tornar não significativos. Isso pode acontecer por vários motivos — por exemplo, o tamanho da amostra pode ser insuficiente para detectar diferenças reais, ou os fatores podem estar interligados de forma complexa (como colinearidade), ou o número de casos de infecção pode ser muito pequeno para permitir conclusões firmes.

As we saw in the previous section, the interference of laser beams creates a spatially varying potential that traps ultracold atoms in a periodic pattern—this is the optical lattice. In particular, the configuration shown in Fig. 2(a) is designed to generate a specific interference field $ V_3(x, y) $, which contributes to shaping the overall lattice potential. When combined with other laser fields (not shown here), this setup produces the full lattice potential $ V(x, y) $, whose energy landscape is plotted in Fig. 2(b) in units of the recoil energy $ E_R = \hbar^2 k^2 / 2m $, a natural energy scale in optical lattices determined by the laser wavevector $ k $ and atomic mass $ m $.

Now, what makes this lattice special? Look closely at the pattern in Fig. 2(b): it’s not just a simple square grid. The intensity and shape of the potential vary in such a way that certain tunneling pathways between neighboring sites are modified. Specifically, the diagonal tunneling amplitudes—how easily atoms can hop between next-nearest-neighbor (nnn) sites—are no longer uniform across the lattice. Instead, they alternate in strength depending on the local potential depth and geometry.

This leads us to the key idea: by carefully tuning the relative intensities of the laser beams that form the interference pattern, we can selectively suppress or enhance tunneling along certain diagonals. The result is a lattice where the effective tunneling rates differ between two interpenetrating sublattices—imagine a checkerboard where black squares have strong diagonal connections, while white squares have weak ones, or vice versa. This is precisely what is illustrated in Fig. 2(c): the **checkerboard lattice**.

Why is this useful? Because it gives us direct control over the ratio of tunneling amplitudes. Recall that in such systems, the dominant tunneling occurs between nearest neighbors (nn), denoted by $ t_1 $, and next-nearest neighbors (nnn), denoted by $ t_2 $. In a standard square lattice, $ t_2 $ is typically much smaller than $ t_1 $, but in this engineered checkerboard setup, we can tune their ratio $ t_2 / t_1 $ by adjusting the intensity of one of the laser fields—specifically $ V_2 $, as mentioned in the text.

Let’s pause to clarify: when we say “adjust the value of $ V_2 $”, we mean changing the depth or phase of one component of the optical potential. This alters the local wavefunction overlap between adjacent sites, thereby modifying the probability of quantum tunneling. So even though $ V_1 $ and $ V_3 $ are held fixed, tweaking $ V_2 $ reshapes the energy landscape just enough to change $ t_2 $ relative to $ t_1 $.

Now, here’s the big picture: when $ t_2 $ becomes comparable to $ t_1 $, something remarkable happens. The resulting magnetic interactions—mediated through virtual tunneling processes—lead to a situation where competing exchange couplings $ J_1 $ and $ J_2 $ are also comparable. This brings us into the **strongly frustrated regime**, where $ J_2 / J_1 \sim 1 $. Frustration means that the system cannot simultaneously minimize all its interaction energies, leading to a vast number of nearly degenerate ground states and potentially exotic quantum phases.

III. THE FRUSTRATED J1-J2 HEISENBERG  
MODELS  

So how do we connect this engineered optical lattice to magnetism? The answer lies in a beautiful chain of physical reasoning that links atomic motion to spin interactions.

Imagine loading ultracold fermionic atoms—such as lithium-6 or potassium-40—into this checkerboard optical lattice. These atoms have two accessible internal states, usually different hyperfine levels, which we can label as “up” ($ |\uparrow\rangle $) and “down” ($ |\downarrow\rangle $). These two states will serve as our effective **spin-1/2 degrees of freedom**, even though they aren’t actual electron spins. This is a common trick in quantum simulation: use controllable quantum systems to mimic others that are harder to study.

Now, suppose we tune the system so that there is exactly **one atom per lattice site**. This is called **integer filling**. Furthermore, we make the on-site repulsion $ U $ very strong compared to the tunneling rates $ t_1 $ and $ t_2 $. In this regime, known as the **Mott insulator**, atoms are essentially pinned to their sites because it would cost too much energy to double-occupy any site. This suppresses charge motion, but interestingly, **spin dynamics still remain active** through virtual hopping processes.

To describe this system mathematically, we start with the **Fermi-Hubbard Hamiltonian**, which captures both kinetic energy (tunneling) and interaction energy:

$$
H = - t_1 \sum_{\langle i,j \rangle,\sigma} (c^\dagger_{i\sigma} c_{j\sigma} + \text{h.c.}) 
- t_2 \sum_{\langle\langle i,j \rangle\rangle,\sigma} (c^\dagger_{i\sigma} c_{j\sigma} + \text{h.c.}) 
+ U \sum_i n_{i\uparrow} n_{i\downarrow},
\tag{5}
$$

Let’s unpack this equation piece by piece.

- $ c_{i\sigma} $ is the **fermion annihilation operator**: it removes a fermion with spin $ \sigma $ (either $ \uparrow $ or $ \downarrow $) from lattice site $ i $. Its Hermitian conjugate $ c^\dagger_{i\sigma} $ creates one.
- $ n_{i\sigma} = c^\dagger_{i\sigma} c_{i\sigma} $ counts the number of fermions with spin $ \sigma $ on site $ i $, so $ n_{i\uparrow} n_{i\downarrow} $ is 1 only if both spin-up and spin-down fermions are present on the same site—this is the double occupancy.
- The first two terms describe **quantum tunneling**: atoms can hop between nearest-neighbor sites (denoted $ \langle i,j \rangle $) with amplitude $ t_1 $, or between next-nearest-neighbor sites (denoted $ \langle\langle i,j \rangle\rangle $) with amplitude $ t_2 $. The “h.c.” stands for Hermitian conjugate, ensuring the Hamiltonian is self-adjoint.
- $ U $ is the **on-site repulsive interaction energy**, which penalizes double occupancy. It can be tuned experimentally using **Feshbach resonances**, a powerful technique that uses magnetic fields to adjust interatomic scattering lengths.

Now, in the **Mott insulating regime**, where $ t_1, t_2 \ll U $, actual particle movement is highly suppressed. But quantum mechanics allows for **virtual processes**: an atom can briefly hop to a neighboring site and then hop back, as long as it doesn’t violate energy conservation over long times. These virtual hoppings don’t change the charge configuration but *can* flip spins.

To extract the effective low-energy physics, we apply a theoretical tool called the **Schrieffer-Wolff transformation**. This is a canonical transformation that integrates out high-energy charge fluctuations (like double occupancies) and yields an effective Hamiltonian acting only on the spin degrees of freedom.

After performing this transformation, the resulting physics is captured by the **J1-J2 Heisenberg model**:

$$
H = J_1 \sum_{\langle i,j \rangle} \mathbf{S}_i \cdot \mathbf{S}_j + J_2 \sum_{\langle\langle i,j \rangle\rangle} \mathbf{S}_j \cdot \mathbf{S}_j.
\tag{6}
$$

Here, $ \mathbf{S}_i $ is the spin-1/2 operator at site $ i $, and the sums run over nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor pairs, respectively.

The exchange couplings are given by:
$$
J_i = \frac{4 t_i^2}{U}, \quad \text{for } i = 1,2.
$$

So $ J_1 $ comes from nearest-neighbor tunneling $ t_1 $, and $ J_2 $ from next-nearest-neighbor tunneling $ t_2 $. Since both are proportional to $ t_i^2 / U $, they are always positive under our assumptions—meaning both interactions are **antiferromagnetic**: neighboring spins prefer to point in opposite directions.

But here’s the catch: when both $ J_1 $ and $ J_2 $ are significant, they compete. On a square lattice, $ J_1 $ favors a Néel-type antiferromagnetic order (alternating up/down spins), but $ J_2 $ introduces diagonal interactions that want to align spins along rows or columns in a striped pattern. When $ J_2 / J_1 \sim 0.5 $, this competition becomes intense—this is the **strongly frustrated regime**.

At this point, the system cannot settle into a simple ordered state. Instead, it may form a **quantum spin liquid**, a highly entangled phase with no long-range magnetic order, even at zero temperature. While numerical and analytical studies have proposed several candidate states—such as gapped $ \mathbb{Z}_2 $ spin liquids or gapless Dirac spin liquids—there is still no universal agreement on the exact nature of the ground state in this regime [26–28].

entre as séries e os exercícios foi de aproximadamente 90 segundos(2). 
A 1RM foi determinada tipicamente dentro de quatro-seis experi -
mentações(9). Primeiramente, o avaliado realizava um aquecimento de 
seis a 10 repetições, com aproximadamente 50% de sua carga máxima 
estimada para a primeira tentativa no teste. Após o aquecimento, o 
sujeito tinha um intervalo de dois minutos e, em seguida, o avaliado 
iniciava o teste. 
Os sujeitos foram orientados a tentarem completar duas repetições. 
Caso fossem completadas duas repetições na primeira tentativa, ou 
mesmo se não fosse completada sequer uma repetição, uma segun -
da tentativa era oportunizada após um intervalo de recuperação de 
três a cinco minutos, com a carga superior (primeira possibilidade) ou 
inferior (segunda possibilidade) àquela utilizada na tentativa anterior. 
Este procedimento foi repetido novamente em uma terceira e última 
tentativa, caso ainda a carga de 1RM não tivesse sido determinada, 
sendo que o intervalo entre os exercícios foi de cinco minutos(2). Todos 
os procedimentos de teste foram supervisionados rigorosamente, e o 
incentivo uniforme foi oferecido a todos os sujeitos. 
Primeiramente, foi executado o teste na cadeira extensora e em 
seguida na rosca direta de bíceps, sendo que a ordem de execução 
obedeceu ao tamanho do maior grupo muscular agonista envolvido. 
A forma e a técnica de execução foram padronizadas conforme Fai -
genbaum e Westcott (20). Um movimento mal sucedido era definido 
quando o mesmo não era realizado em sua amplitude completa nas 
duas repetições(2). 
Idade cronológica e maturação sexual
A idade cronológica foi expressa na sua forma milesimal conforme 
os procedimentos apresentados por Healy et al.(21). A maturação bioló-
gica foi indicada através do método de análise das características sexu-
ais secundárias, sendo esta realizada pela análise do desenvolvimento 
genital e da pilosidade pubiana na forma de autoavaliação mediante 
o uso dos padrões fotográficos propostos por Tanner(22) e modificadas 
por Matsudo(23), e pela análise visual da pilosidade axilar.
Análise estatística
A análise de normalidade da distribuição dos dados foi realizada por 
meio do teste de Shapiro Wilk no qual a significância adotada foi de p 
≤ 0,05. Para a caracterização da amostra foi utilizada estatística descri -
tiva (média, desvio padrão, mediana, mínimo e máximo). A associação 
entre as variáveis foi averiguada mediante o emprego do coeficiente 
de correlação de Spearman, a significância estatística estabelecida para 
as análises foi de p < 0,01; p ≤ 0,05. Para a realização das análises foi 
utilizado o programa SPSS 13.0.
